children.author: disgruntledphd2
children.text:
> Older IPOs like Facebook felt different, like the hard part had been done, and they just had to scale.

Facebook were actually forced to IPO, because they had too many shareholders to remain private. They were super generous with allowing early employees to sell equity, and the laws required them to list once they passed 500 (i think) external shareholders.

This got changed in later legislation, which is part of the reason that companies like Stripe have been able to remain private for so much longer.

That being said, I agree with basically everything else in your comment, including the feelings around this.

LLMs (and Claude more specifically) are wonderful products, but I'm not convinced that they can justify their valuations over time.

> They have infinite money to burn so they aren't going to optimize.

IPOs aren't the magical moment that they were in decades past. You get to answer to a bunch of retirement fund managers and "the market", meaning less-savvy retail investors. You have to open up your books.

It seems like Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. are doing an IPO because they are literally out of other options. Older IPOs like Facebook felt different, like the hard part had been done, and they just had to scale. There's a difference in selling something because you want to, versus selling something because you have to. Facebook was just relying on the idea that they were a platform that more people would inevitably sign up for. For the most part, they did. It seemed obvious. They likely could have continued on by simply operating privately, but the IPO gave them capital to dominate the market.

Anthropic and other hyperscalers cannot continue on privately. They're facing a systemic shortage of capital to achieve their goals. They need the infrastructure, and there's not enough capacity to make enough for all of these companies to survive.

children.text:
> That's not how it works

I know that's not how it works, I'm explaining why they do it in a particular way because of what would happen if they did it the other way.

Suppose a company could transfer an asset to an employee and have its value set as the employer's cost.

That's not how it works...The value would be the FMV at the time of the transfer to the employee. The cost basis would be the employer's cost. The income to the employee would be the net difference.

What would happen if any employer could do that with any employee and any asset?

They can't, because tax laws have addressed this situation for almost 100 years...

there is a separate carve out for "employee discounts", which is essentially the employer offering its employees its own products for something in the neighborhood of its own cost.

That carveout only applies to products being offered for the employee's own consumption unrelated to the needs of the business. Internal use of a company's own products for the needs of the business does not result in additional GAAP or tax deductions (meaning, if that product cost X to make/provide but they charge external customers Y, the only deduction is X, not Y).

IRS rules should never be used as an example of how accounting "should" work. They're full of politics and the implications of the rules on tax avoidance.

Suppose a company could transfer an asset to an employee and have its value set as the employer's cost. A company could make a bunch of volatile investments and see which ones pay off. Then the ones that go south get sold back into the market as a tax loss and the ones that do well get transferred as compensation to employees at the purchase price instead of the current value, reducing the tax liability of both the employer (no taxable gain) and the employee (less taxable income). What would happen if any employer could do that with any employee and any asset?

Conversely, there is a separate carve out for "employee discounts", which is essentially the employer offering its employees its own products for something in the neighborhood of its own cost. Why? It's not in any way a principled accounting distinction, it's because it's harder to use for tax avoidance at scale, because then a soap company can give its employees a discount on soap, but people only need a finite amount of soap and then the soap company can't use it for cars and real estate and stocks.

children.author: ElevenLathe
children.text: Your AI token bill isn't a "benefit", it's just an expense, just like all the other software subscriptions your work pays for.

In the US, the IRS doesn't see it that way, at least when it comes to fringe benefits as a part of employee compensation. https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employe... says, "In general, the amount the employer must include is the amount by which the fair market value of the benefits is more than the sum of what the employee paid for it plus any amount that the law excludes."

As an example, as I understand it, if a hotel chain allows an employee to stay in one of their hotels for free when they go on vacation, the tax value of that benefit is what they would have charged someone for that hotel room, not how much it increased the hotel's costs to have one more hotel room full — which is generally almost nothing.

Of course, the IRS does agree with you when it comes to expenditures that are for the employer's benefit, rather than the employee's. If it didn't, almost all companies would have negative profits from the IRS's point of view.

children.text:
No, one thing that would happen is that many projects would never be undertaken - basically, there's latent demand for software that would simply go unmet, because of resource constraints.

I was recently involved in a case like this - we had a critical part of our system based on a dependency that's no longer maintained. Previously, we would have just carried on for a year or more, living with the limitations until it was much closer to being entirely untenable, because rewriting the code in question would have been a multi-month project involving multiple developers, QA, and management time. But now, the code in question was migrated in a few days using AI, along with a suite of new tests in addition to our existing ones, that gave us a lot of confidence in the results. The productivity improvement here is at least on the order of 25x, possibly higher.

But most developers aren't sitting at their desks operating at a 25x pace all day, every day, so average productivity improvement is going to be lower. And of course, some use of AI will be suboptimal or problematic: waste due to e.g. duplicate development which happens when development is so easy, or costs for cleanup of mistakes.

We also now have a slew of AI-generated internal tools, most of which would never have been developed before. Many of them are very useful, the kind of thing that's on your eternal wishlist but never gets done. Some are kinda useless, so represent wasted resources. It's difficult to measure the productivity benefit of all this, because you'd have to compare it to the non-existent company without those tools.

Sorry, I know this is the story, but am I expected to believe that Anthropic would need 20,000+ engineers in their org without their use of AI? I do not believe that is close to true.

I mean, just what I did this morning with Claude would have taken me 2 weeks on my own. So 20x is pretty reasonable for certain types of engineering.

But it's also true that when I'm working on 2 things at once, the bottleneck is me. I'm spending all my time giving Claude direction that it can't give itself.

So you basically have to separate out the tasks where AI can produce a 20x productivity boost, and the stuff where it can't help at all.

There's still so much stuff where it can't help at all, you need real human employees for that. That's why Anthropic is continuing to hire at breakneck pace.

children.text:
Xerox made quite a bit of money selling laser printers for desktop publishing, too, a lot more than they ever spent on PARC.

I don't think it's accurate that "almost all the money in personal computing was made in mobile". Quite a bit of money was made in personal computing before the iPhone, and quite a bit of money has been made in non-mobile computing since the iPhone.

I also don't think it's accurate that mobile "didn't use any of these ideas". Android's UI is not quite as close to Smalltalk-78 as what I'm using right now, but you still have pointers, scrollbars, text selections, proportional fonts, vertical-line cursors, buttons, menus, object-oriented programming, sometimes a bytecode interpreter, and even windows. You just don't have as much freedom with where you position the windows. Android's UI is still a lot closer to Smalltalk-78 than it is to, for example, acme, GENESYS, the ITS HACTRN, FORTH, or PDP-11 Unix.

It’s true employees at the big AI firms are living in the future, but since this disclosure is in marketing materials to sell their stock to investors, it’s important to note that almost all the money in personal computing was made in mobile which didn’t use any of these ideas, and in desktop computing the money was made by Microsoft who treated the GUI as ancillary and competed on distribution.

They're dogfooding the way Xerox PARC was dogfooding in the 01970s.

By giving hundreds of workers each a powerful desk-sized Alto minicomputer for their own needs, with a high-end graphical display, they gained insight into what desktop personal computing would look like 15 years later, enough insight to shape it profoundly. It's been 55 years, and although multitouch screens are proliferating, I'm still typing this on a keyboard hooked up to a framebuffer-driven display with a mouse hooked up to it, displaying hypertext, festooned with windows, icons, and a mouse that moves an onscreen pointer at the same 135° angle they settled on 55 years ago, positioning a vertical line to indicate the insertion point, with scrollbars. The display has twice as many pixels, the pixels are color, the mouse pointer is white rather than black, the screen is a flat LCD, the scrollbars are on the right, and the cursor blinks, but it's very recognizably descended from https://smalltalkzoo.computerhistory.org/HOPL-St78.html rather than, for example, ITS or GENESYS.

Only people with the luxury of unlimited zero-cost CPU cycles had a chance of seeing what the future looked like, and that allowed them to find out what worked and what didn't work in that environment. Nowadays, the regular workers who don't have the luxury of unlimited zero-cost tokens are manually reviewing voluminous AI code, because, even though that's a lot of slow work, they're still much faster programming that way than they were without it. Anthropic, instead, is doing insane things like eliciting a billion lines of Lean proofs to show that existing open-source libraries can't fail their OSS-FUZZ tests — and fixing all the bugs that effort turned up, in the process.

Everyone is saying it is expected, and I agree, but it’s also clear that employees of AI companies spending unlimited zero-cost tokens in their day-to-day work is resulting in products that aren’t usable by the vast majority of regular workers who don’t have this luxury. Dogfooding your product is good but you should also use it with the same constraints that you place on your users, otherwise what signals are you really getting?
